newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey stays distant from Perry's anti-Iraq bid.
newsitem.headline: Turkey stays distant from Perry's anti-Iraq bid.

text.p: NATO ally Turkey gave visiting U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry few concrete signs on Monday of support in his search for a tightening of military and economic pressure against neighbouring Iraq.
Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller repeated earlier comments that Ankara would not allow U.S. jets to use the Incirlik air base in southern Turkey for bombing raids on Iraq if Washington requested it.

"We have already told them that it is not possible for us to accept such a request from Incirlik. This would not be the right approach according to our interests," she told reporters after a working breakfast with Perry.
But Ciller said the Americans had not specifically asked to use Incirlik, a joint Turkish-U.S. base from where Western allied planes patrol a no-fly zone over northern Iraq to protect the Kurds.
"There is no U.S. request. So there is no change in Turkish policy," she said.
Washington used the base during the 1991 Gulf War that ousted Iraqi troops from Kuwait but Turkey's support for the alliance against Baghdad has cost it dearly.
Turkish officials say the coalition effort has cost the country $25 billion in losses from the U.N. sanctions on former leading trade partner Baghdad. Western officials say the figure is less.
Turkey also complains that the no-fly zone has caused a power vacuum in Kurdish-held northern Iraq that has allowed Turkish Kurd rebels to establish themselves there.
Perry was tightlipped. "They were good consultations," he told reporters in a brief statement at Ankara airport, before boarding a U.S. air force C-17 transport plane for further talks in London.

Perry took no questions but aides said a written statement would be distributed later. "He heard, from the government of Turkey, Turkish views on the situation in Iraq," U.S. ambassador Marc Grossman told reporters.
Perry, on a Middle Eastern tour to reactivate the Gulf War alliance against President Saddam Hussein, received more solid backing from Kuwait, which he visited on Sunday.
The Gulf state on Monday approved a U.S. request relayed by Perry to deploy additional ground troops there.
"Yes, we have agreed," a Kuwaiti official, who declined to be identified, said by telephone. He said the deployment would be a little less than the 5,000 troops proposed by Washington.

The Clinton administration on Friday announced it had ordered 5,000 army troops from Fort Hood, Texas to join forces already in the Gulf in preparation for possible military action against Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.
Perry's diplomatic offensive has also taken him to Saudi Arabia and Bahrain.
He held talks with Turkey's armed forces chief and President Suleyman Demirel on Monday but a meeting with Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan was conspicuous by its absence.
Washington has kept Erbakan at arms' length since he took power in late June.

A senior member of Erbakan's Welfare Party said any meeting with Perry would not have been in line with protocol. "The U.S. defence secretary meets the (Turkish) foreign minister or the defence minister when he comes," State Minister Mehmet Altinsoy said. "A prime minister meets a prime minister," he said.
